cim: European Union Laws Fail to Guarantee Public Participation in Public-Sector AI Development
cim_eredeti: European Union Laws Fail to Guarantee Public Participation in Public-Sector AI Development
szoveg_eredeti:
European Union Laws Fail to Guarantee Public Participation in Public-Sector AI Development

A doctrinal legal investigation published in Cambridge Forum on AI: Law and Governance examines whether public participation can realistically serve as an operational mechanism to reduce risks in public-sector artificial intelligence systems across the European Union. Although public administration literature and policy proposals frequently champion public involvement as a potential silver bullet to address algorithmic bias, opacity, and democratic deficits, the study demonstrates that the legal architecture of the European Union currently provides no functional avenues for natural or legal persons to influence the design and development of public-sector algorithmic tools. While public administrations across thirty European countries documented nine hundred and forty cases of artificial intelligence deployment in 2024, representing an increase of nearly thirty percent compared to figures reported at the end of 2022, citizen involvement remains nonexistent. This disconnect leaves the general public completely detached from critical decisions that govern the development of algorithmic systems increasingly deployed in sensitive administrative operations, ranging from routine traffic offense enforcement to critical decisions in tax collection, welfare benefit processing, crime risk forecasting, and asylum procedures.

The study establishes that the core rationale behind citizen engagement stems from documented evidence of widespread societal harms generated by artificial intelligence deployments, which frequently exacerbate historical biases, generate discriminatory outcomes, and disproportionately affect disadvantaged and marginalized groups. Legal and administrative scholars have long argued that consulting the public before public bodies deploy automated systems could prevent administrations from pursuing projects bound to fail from lack of societal acceptance, incorporate varied communal values into public service technologies, and identify sensitive vulnerabilities early during the development phase. Furthermore, direct engagement during early design stages has been theorized to confer democratic legitimacy, preserve public trust, prevent the corporate takeover of public infrastructures when private vendors build public software, and ensure algorithmic systems reflect public interest rather than narrow bureaucratic or commercial imperatives. Nevertheless, while conceptual defenses of participatory governance in artificial intelligence are pervasive throughout academic literature, legal scholarship had previously left the practical, doctrinal avenues governing such participation unexamined, leaving a substantial gap between theoretical aspirations and existing statutory administrative law.

To assess whether traditional European administrative law could accommodate public engagement in algorithmic design, the author examined both rulemaking and individual decision-making procedures anchored in primary treaties, European Union secondary legislation, and the jurisprudence of the Court of Justice of the European Union. In the domain of administrative rulemaking, where public bodies enact general norms or authorize the institutional deployment of algorithmic tools, public participation does not constitute a legally enforceable individual right. Although the European Commission systematically conducts open consultations, as observed during the revisions of public procurement directives, stakeholder hearings on the Artificial Intelligence Act, and the drafting of the General-Purpose AI Code of Practice involving more than one thousand participants, these mechanisms remain informal and non-compulsory under established European Union case law. Furthermore, these participatory exercises target structured representative associations and civil society groups rather than individual citizens, meaning that administrative rulemaking fails to offer a dependable, open gateway for ordinary members of the public to directly influence how automated systems are designed.

When examining traditional administrative decision-making, the investigation identified equally insurmountable legal barriers within the defensive rights granted to citizens under the umbrella of good administration. The fundamental right to be heard cannot legally function in the context of system development because it requires a strict bilateral legal relationship between an administrative authority and an individual addressee whose legal sphere is directly and negatively affected by an administrative measure. Because public-sector artificial intelligence systems are built to process a vast multitude of future administrative tasks across general populations rather than a single individualized dispute, system development operates completely outside the perimeter of individual decision-making procedures. Even under the expanded doctrinal scope established in the Al-Jubail jurisprudence concerning hybrid regulations, acts performed during algorithmic development produce effects that are far too indirect and preliminary to confer standing. By the time an administrative agency takes an individual adverse measure against an individual using an algorithmic system, the underlying architecture has already been locked in, rendering the right to be heard entirely ineffective for shaping the software itself.

The companion defensive right to access administrative documents presents a seemingly broader pathway, yet it also collapses as an effective participatory vehicle upon closer doctrinal scrutiny. Under European Union administrative law, the right of access to documents allows any natural or legal person residing within the Union to inspect files held by European Union institutions without demonstrating a direct legal or economic interest, potentially encompassing outsourced technical documents. However, this statutory right is strictly limited by two major legal exceptions: the commercial interest exception, which protects proprietary algorithms, commercial data, and corporate trade secrets when public authorities contract out technology development to private software companies, and the internal documents exception, which shields in-house administrative deliberations whenever disclosure risks impairing bureaucratic decision-making. Even where non-confidential records can be obtained, the right of access to documents functions merely as a passive mechanism for information retrieval; it contains no corresponding legal obligation compelling administrative bodies to incorporate, evaluate, or respond to the empirical critiques or values offered by the citizens reviewing those materials.

Turning to public procurement law, the research evaluated whether citizen participation could be integrated when public authorities purchase commercially available off-the-shelf software or contract private developers to construct customized algorithmic platforms. The analysis found that existing European procurement directives and financial regulations applicable to European Union institutions do not accommodate public or civil society intervention within procurement operations or contract performance phases. Historically constructed around the interaction between contracting authorities and bidding economic operators to safeguard equal treatment, market efficiency, and non-distortion of competition, European procurement law defines participation exclusively as the right of economic operators to compete for contracts. While member states maintain limited administrative discretion during statutory transposition to require transparency, publish procurement contracts, or expand preliminary market consultations to include technical experts and civic organizations, such avenues remain entirely indirect, precluding ordinary citizens and civic monitoring groups from directly collaborating in negotiating technical specifications or managing so
